title: The three lines: right, left, and the middle line that reaches the inner Keser
overview:
In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* in three lines. On the right, *chachma*, *chesed* and *netzach*: *chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for, "it's the thought that counts", and so leans to kindness. On the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod*: *bina* looks at the outside, draws distinctions, and is nitpicky. Each branch is separate from its source, which is why a high-minded idea loses force by the time it has to go out knocking on doors in the cold.

The two sides come together only through the middle line. *Daas* sees both as tools and makes a judgment call for this person, a human thing no computer can do; *tiferes* is mercy after the verdict, Yaakov's way of giving a ladder out of the mud; *yesod* decides between *netzach* and *hod*, the kidneys that say yes and no. The middle line can join them because it reaches the inner *Keser*, the will with no reason, all or nothing. The *paroches* is where that will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

terms.gloss: lines: the three lines of a partzuf, chachma, chesed and netzach on the right, bina, gevura and hod on the left, daas, tiferes and yesod in the middle
the Keser within the Keser: the inner, essential will, which does not split into lines
acknowledgement: holding back, caution, giving up one's strength before what is bigger
the daas that tilts: it sees both sides and decides how much of each, for this person and this situation
mercy: it comes after the verdict, and lets the person off because the goal is that he improve
the kidneys that advise: netzach and hod, which say yes and no on how to carry out a decision
the weighing of the mind: the whole middle line, which makes a judgment call
the middle bar: the pole through all the boards of the Mishkan; the middle line, one through every level
the hidden reason for the will: chachma of Keser, hidden because the will covers it, and really a taste of delight
the days of old: the middos of the will and delight, the original dream before it is brought down to what is possible
the curtain between the Holy and the Holy of Holies: the screen between the essential will and the will that has a form
the membrane of air, which he calls the arachnoid membrane: the screen through which the essential delight reaches the faculties

sections.title: Three lines: the inner Keser does not divide, its outer side does
sections.summary: In *Tikun* the *sefiros* stand as a *partzuf* (a stature) in three lines, right, left and middle. The inner *Keser*, the essential will, does not split into lines; from its outer side, already *chachma* of *Keser*, they divide.

phrases.he: (כא) ובזה יובן כללות ענין ההתכללות דג' קוין דנאצלים,
חח''ן מימין ובג''ה משמאל ודת''י באמצע כו'
phrases.en: that when the *sefiros* go out, *chachma*, *chesed*, *netzach* is on the right, *bina*, *gevura*, *hod* is on the left, and then *daas*, *tiferes*, *yesod* stays in the middle.

blocks.text:
Now he continues and explains the *kavin* (the three lines): how the *sefiros* (the Divine attributes) split up into three lines. We already explained the difference between *Tohu* (the world of Chaos) and *Tikun* (the world of repair). In *Tohu* it is the way of the *nekudos* (the separate points), and in *Tikun* it becomes a *partzuf* (lit. face; a stature of the *sefiros*). And a *partzuf* means that there are three lines.

When the *sefiros* go out, *chachma* (wisdom), *chesed* (kindness) and *netzach* (victory) are on the right; *bina* (understanding), *gevura* (might, restraint) and *hod* (acknowledgement) are on the left; and *daas* (knowledge), *tiferes* (beauty) and *yesod* (foundation) stay in the middle.

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב בפרדס דפנימית הכתר הנקרא כתר שבכתר,
לא נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: That doesn't split up into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: בחינת חיצוניות שבו,
phrases.en: but from the *chitzoniyus* of the *ratzon* already,

phrases.he: ממנו מתחלק לג' קוין
והוא מבחינת חכמה שבכתר כו', וכידוע בכונות דהגדול הגבור והנורא כו'.

blocks.text:
As it says in the *Pardes*, the *pnimiyus* (the inner side) of *Keser*, called *Keser sheb'Keser*, is the actual inner *ratzon* (will). That is like the *nekuda* (the point): that you want it, the *etzem* (essence) thing. It does not split up into three lines.

But from the *chitzoniyus* (the outer side) of the *ratzon*, already, it divides into three lines. There it already becomes associated like a *partzuf* in *yosher* (the straight line). As we said about *Arich Anpin*, it is *davka* (specifically) in the form of *Chabad* and the six *middos* (emotional attributes) that it becomes *yosher*.

And this is from *chachma* of *Keser*, as is known from the *kavanos* (intentions) of "the great, the mighty and the awesome": those are the three lines in the *Keser*. "The great" is *chesed*; "and the mighty" is *gevura*; and the *heh* (the letter meaning "the") means "the one", in a way a *hispashtus* (spreading forth). That is the way it is in *Keser*.

sections.title: The right line and the left: chachma looks past the form, bina at it
sections.summary: On the right, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma* and *netzach* a branch of *chesed*, each separate from its source; on the left, *bina*, *gevura* and *hod* are the opposite. *Chachma* looks past the outside to what it stands for and so leans to kindness; *bina* looks at the outside, makes distinctions and leans to judgement.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים, הנה בחינת התכללות הקוין ימין ושמאל הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דוקא
phrases.en: The right and the left lines are connected through the middle line.

blocks.text: The explanation of the matter: the inclusion of the lines, right and left, is *davka* through the middle line. The right and the left lines are connected only through the middle line.

phrases.he: והענין הוא דקו הימין חח''ן, הרי החסד ענף החכמה ומובדל הימנה
phrases.en: On the right line, *chesed* is a branch of *chachma*, but it's separate from it.

phrases.he: והוא מה שנסתעף החסד מצד השכל והטעם, שמטה כלפי חסד
phrases.en: This is when, because of a reason, you lean towards *chesed*.

phrases.he: בדבר מורכב כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: On the right line, **chesed is a branch of chachma, but it's separate from it**. This is the *chesed* that branches out because of the intellect and the reason: **because of a reason, you lean towards chesed**. It is not an *etzem chesed* (essential kindness); your *sechel* (intellect) causes the *chesed*.

blocks.title: The right hand gives
blocks.text: This is like the right arm being on the same side as the right side of the brain. Usually you hold something with your left hand, and you take and give things with your right hand. That is one of the reasons the right hand is a *mashal* (analogy) for *chesed*, and it is on the same side as *chachma*.

In general, *chachma* leans towards *chesed*. Why? The *inyan* (concept) of *chachma* is to look behind, past the *chitzoniyus*, past the form. *Bina* looks at the external form, and *chachma* looks at what it represents, the abstract thing behind it. So *chachma* tends to lean towards *chesed*, and *bina* tends to lean towards *gevura*.

blocks.title: It's the thought that counts
blocks.text: As we spoke about before, if somebody gives a gift to somebody, and you look into it, you say, "It's the thought that counts." That is what *chachma* looks at. You look deeper at what this represents, and you appreciate it very much.

blocks.title: Looking past a person's deeds
blocks.text: The same with a person. If you look at a person, you look past it even if they are not so good outwardly, even if what they are doing is not so good. You look at their inner motivation, at how inside they are a person like you, and you can relate to them: really they are just misguided. That is like a *chachma*.

*Bina* focuses on the external thing. And if you focus on the external, then, as we said, you are never going to be able to find a gift that is a proper representation of the love you are trying to express. If you are going to be *medakdek* (exacting) on the outside, it is never going to be perfect. You are always going to find the flaw, always find that it falls short.

The same with a person. If you are going to be *medakdek*, "there is no righteous man on earth": if you are exacting about a person's actions, you are always going to be able to find something wrong with the way they are externally, especially with how they live up to what you could expect from them. That's true.

So you could look at it either way. *Chachma* says: since it is impossible to properly represent the feeling in the external thing, we should just look past it. It's the thought that counts; there is this *etzem* connection, and it doesn't really matter how we express it. The main thing is that it's there.

*Bina* looks at the external thing and says, "But I want it to come out. I want you to make an effort to make something that is a meaningful expression of whatever it is you are trying to convey. I want you to act in a way that's befitting who you really are, to do things that will express the relationship that we have." So it is very nitpicky. That is why *chachma* tends to lean towards *chesed*.

blocks.title: The poor person
blocks.text: Say a person looks at a poor person. If he looks at him from the side of *chachma*, he feels that he should really be nice to him. He finds a common ground, how he really relates to the person, and he can sympathize, and so he wants to give him *tzedaka* (charity) or something; or intellectually he understands that it is good to be nice to him.

phrases.he: וכן הנצח ענף החסד,
phrases.en: and likewise, *netzach* is an *anaf* of *chesed*,

phrases.he: מובדל הימנו.
phrases.en: but it's also separate from the *chesed*.

phrases.he: דהיינו מצד החסד יחויב בחינת הניצוח להביא החסד למעשה בפועל ממש כו'

blocks.text: And likewise, *netzach* is an *anaf* (a branch) of *chesed*, but it is also separate from the *chesed*. From the side of the *chesed*, *netzach* is required, to bring the *chesed* to actual deed. The *inyan* of *chesed* is *hispashtus*: you want to get something out. If you want to express something to somebody, or give something to somebody, there is definitely going to be opposition when you want to bring it out in deed, to figure out how to do it. That is the *inyan* of *netzach*.

blocks.title: The father teaching his son
blocks.text: There is always going to be a fight with the *kli* (vessel), like the *mashal* in *Tanya* of a father trying to teach his son. From the side of the *chesed*, he wants to teach his son what he knows, his *chachma*, but it is hard for him: he has to bring it down to the son's level. The *inyan* of *netzach* is that if you want to bring it across, you are going to have to work to overcome the language barrier and the different backgrounds, to bring it out in a way the person will appreciate.

blocks.title: Running after him to help
blocks.text: The simple thing is the right leg. If a person wants to go give *chesed* to a guy, the *chesed* obligates him really to run after the guy, even, to help him. That is really a *netzach* thing. If there is some kind of obstacle, the *chesed* says, "Well, really you should even have *netzach*; you should even be willing to fight for what's right."

But as he is going to say, in the right line and in the left line they are detached. So you see in practice that a person, in theory, can be very high-minded from the side of his *chachma*. When it comes to the emotion, he does not really feel so enthusiastic anymore, and by the time it comes to *netzach*, to actually having to run after somebody, it is a lot less. Still, it obligates him: a person should do these things.

blocks.title: Mivtzaim in the cold
blocks.text:
Like *mivtzaim* (outreach campaigns). A person knows from the side of *chachma* that it is right to go and help other Jews, and so he feels a *chesed*, that they should be helped. But when it comes to actually going and doing it, and it is difficult, that is a *netzach* thing. They have to overcome obstacles to raise money and get the things and go out; there is the time, it is cold, they have to find the people. It is uncomfortable for a lot of people to go around knocking on doors, giving out menorahs or whatever it is.

That is the *netzach*. The *chesed* obligates it; it really says that you should do it. But it is detached, so that it loses some of its *koach* (power), as he is going to say.

phrases.he: וקו השמאל היפוכו,
phrases.en: the left line is the opposite of everything in the right line,

phrases.he: כמו שכל המטה כלפי דין שנסתעף הימנו מידת הדין כו'
כך בינה גבורה כו'
phrases.en: So too is *bina gevura*, that *bina* leans towards *gevura*,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב אני בינה, לי גבורה כו'
phrases.en: I am *bina* and *gevura* is mine,

phrases.he: דהחכמה נוטה לחסדים
ובינה מינה דינין כו'
phrases.en: that from *bina* comes out *dinin*.

phrases.he: (וכמו שכתוב בעץ חיים דאבא מקור החסדים
phrases.en: that *Abba*'s the source of the *chassadim*.

phrases.he: ואימא מקור כל הגבורות כו' וכידוע)
phrases.en: and *Ima* is the *makor* of all the *gevuros*

blocks.text: The left line is the opposite of everything in the right line: an intellect that leans towards *din* (judgement), from which the attribute of judgement branches out. So too is *bina gevura*: *bina* leans towards *gevura*, as it says, "I am *bina*, *gevura* is mine." For *chachma* leans to the *chassadim* (kindnesses), and from *bina* the *dinin* (judgements) come out.

As it says in *Etz Chaim*, *Abba* is the source of the *chassadim*. The *inyan* of *chachma* is that you look into the abstract thing; it is the *inyan* of grasping the *mahus* (the what-it-is), always what is abstract, and that always causes *chassadim*. When you understand something in a way of *chachma*, you see how it really applies to everything, and you see the connection between things. The nature of *chachma* is always to break barriers and go deeper and deeper, to the essence, which transcends boundaries and limitations.

*Bina* is the opposite: to define it, make it very compartmentalized and draw sharp distinctions. So if you want to talk, you have to use *bina* to figure out words to name exactly what you want to say, so people can get what you are talking about. But then, to really understand what a person is saying, you also have to have *chachma*, to read between the lines and pull out what he is really saying. So you need a combination of both.

blocks.title: Living the story
blocks.text: Take a person reading. (Later on we will talk about *chachma* and *bina* and how they deal with language and thought and speech.) If he just knows the literal definition of the words, that is a *bina* thing. But when a person reads and doesn't even realize he is reading anymore, it is as if he is living the story, that is a *chachma* thing: it becomes totally transparent. That is the *inyan* of the *pnimiyus* of the *mochin* (the intellectual faculties), that it is *mamash* (actually) one with its thing.

And *Ima* is the source of all the *gevuros*, because *bina* is the *inyan* of making distinctions and breaking things up, and that is the *inyan* of *gevuros*. First of all, *bina* looks at the *chitzoniyus*, and it also cuts it up and uses a part of it to represent the whole thing. Because it looks at the *chitzoniyus*, it is only the *gilui* (revelation) and not the *etzem*, and that itself is a limited thing, the *inyan* of *gevuros*. And it also cuts it up, which we will talk about later: the *inyan* of the five *gevuros*, the final letters *mem*, *nun*, *tzadi*, *peh*, *chaf*, and so on.
blocks.outOfPlace: Class 78 opens by finishing line 12, which class 77 ended in the middle of.

sections.title: The middle line: daas sees both sides and makes a judgment call
sections.summary: Two ways of looking at anything, past the outside or at it, come together only through *daas*. *Daas* holds both as tools and decides, for this person and this situation, how much of each: a human, subjective judgment no computer can make.

phrases.he: ובחינת ההתכללות דב' קוין הללו שיבואו להתחבר במקום א',
הוא על ידי קו האמצעי דת''י כו'
phrases.en: it's *davka* the middle thing, which is *daas*.

blocks.question: How can *chachma* and *bina*, or *chesed* and *gevura*, come together?
blocks.text: Whenever you approach any situation there are these two sides: you can look at it one way or the other way. So which way do you look at it?

blocks.title: Avraham saw their inner good
blocks.text: You could look at a person the way Avraham looked at people. He saw their inner good: even when they were doing bad things, he realized that they were really being motivated by an inner good desire, and were just expressing it in a bad way. He appreciated their inner potential. If you want to, you can really overlook a person's shortcomings and always see the good, and overlook the fact that he is not acting in a way that is appropriate. Or you could look with *bina*, at the *chitzoniyus*. And neither of those really detracts from the other.
They are two totally different ways of looking at things. So to have them together, it is *davka* the middle thing, which is *daas*.

phrases.he: כמו הדעת שהוא בחינת ממוצע להטות משכל של חסד לשכל של דין, ונקרא דעת נוטה

blocks.text: Like *daas*, which is an intermediary to tilt from an intellect of *chesed* to an intellect of *din*, and is called *daas noteh* (the *daas* that tilts). What *daas* does is that it is able to recognize both. It says: I understand that there is the *chesed* side, that there is the good; I understand that there is also the *gevura* side. On the one hand, the inner thing is good, it's the thought that counts. Say a parent with a child: an essential connection. On the other hand, I don't like the way the person is acting; it makes me uncomfortable. *Daas* is able to understand both of those things, to be *sovel* (to bear) both of them.

And it is also able to see what is best in this situation for this person: the best way to get him to acknowledge that he has this potential, and that it is always there; that you are never going to be able to bring it out all the way perfectly, nobody's perfect. "But I want you to work to bring this out and express it as best as you can in the outside." It makes a personalized thing of what you feel is best in this situation: which side you should focus on, what the proportion should be. So it is a judgment call.

*Daas* is *davka* personal: an opinion, a human thing. You could not have a computer make a decision on the level of *daas*. The *chachma* and the *bina* are a technical thing, but for *daas* you have to say, well, what is our real goal? I know that there are these two sides, and *daas* sees both as tools you can use to motivate, to accomplish things. Whichever side will be most effective, that is the side we will take, or whatever combination of them. That is the *inyan* of *daas noteh*.

phrases.he: (וכמו כי יצר לב כו'
phrases.en: like with the *Mabul*,

phrases.he: שנעשה שכל וטעם לזכות, אשר תחלה היה זה השכל עצמו נוטה כלפי חוב, כמו שכתוב וירא כי רבה רעת כו' וכהאי גוונא וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר)

blocks.text: Like "the inclination of the heart" by the *Mabul* (the Flood): the same intellect was used both for *chesed* and for *din*, the fact that man is bad, is born bad. From the side of the intellect of *chesed* you can look at it and say, so it is not their fault if they sin. Or you could look at it from the side of the intellect of *gevura*: but they are sinning, so that is bad. The same reason became a reason to acquit, where at first that very reason leaned towards guilt, as it says, "And He saw that the evil of man was great."
Everything has two ways you can look at it, and you have to choose which way you are going to look at it. That is *daas*: an opinion, a subjective thing.

phrases.he: ונמצא בדעת יחובר ב' שכליים הפכיים דחסד וגבורה להיות נוטה לחסד באופן זה ולדין באופן זה וכהאי גוונא, גם במקום אחד

blocks.text: So in *daas* the two opposite intellects of *chesed* and *gevura* are joined, to lean to *chesed* in this way and to *din* in that way. *Daas* says that they are both true, but that up to a certain amount we will overlook it, and after that we will not overlook it. You make a judgment: if it is a little thing, and depending on the person and the situation, you overlook it. But you expect a certain amount to come out in the outside, that the person should do it in a good way, that he should put in a certain amount of effort.

This is what we talked about before with the *Kav* (the line of light): the teacher has to measure and decide how much effort he is going to put out, and how much effort he wants the student to put out. How much are you going to come down to the person, and how much do you want the person to put in an effort to come to you? That decision is *davka* a thing of *daas*.

And even in one situation, it is not going to be all or nothing. You can help a little bit and at the same time make him work a little bit. It does not decide sometimes 100% one and sometimes 100% the other; it can make a compromise. In general, the middle line is individualized, and it is a human thing.

sections.title: Tiferes is mercy after the verdict: the attribute of Yaakov
sections.summary: *Tiferes* decides between *chesed* and *gevura* as mercy does: it comes only after judgement, when the person is guilty, and lets him off because the goal is that he improve. That is Yaakov's attribute: give as much help as is needed until he can stand on his own.

phrases.he: וכך מדת התפארת מכריע בין חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: the same way that *tiferes*, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between *chesed* and *gevura*.

phrases.he: שהוא כמו הרחמים,
phrases.en: which that's like mercy,

phrases.he: שאינו אלא אחר מידת הדין,
phrases.en: that after a person is guilty, and there's a problem,

phrases.he: שעם כל זה רחמנות פוטרו,
והיא מדת יעקב כידוע
phrases.en: it's the *midda* of Yaakov,

blocks.text: The same way, **tiferes, which is like a thing of mercy, is an intermediary between chesed and gevura**. It is like mercy, which comes only after the attribute of judgement: **after a person is guilty, and there's a problem**, even so mercy lets him off. You say, "I beg the mercy of the court": after a person was found guilty, then you ask for mercy.

The *inyan* of *rachmanus* (mercy) means that you recognize that the person has a certain good. If there were no hope, no good in the person, you would only feel *gevura*. You recognize that there is some good, and you recognize that it is being messed up. And *rachmanus* says that even though the person really is messed up, "Sometimes I'm going to overlook it, because the person needs the help." Since my real goal is to help the person, it is not really about a judgment system. The laws are not really about who is right. The point is to get the person to improve.

blocks.title: Tests, scores and three strikes
blocks.text: Say a teacher has tests, or three strikes you're out: a whole system, a testing system with scores. The whole purpose of making it is that the person should have to work and the responsibility should be on him. But say he worked really hard and it didn't work out. From the side of *din* you will say, "It doesn't matter. These are the rules. The reason I have to make a strict standard is that if I let people off, people aren't going to work and they're not going to learn." So sometimes you have to say, "I don't care," and even be harsh *davka*, to make an example, to inspire other people to work.

blocks.title: The student below the level of the class
blocks.text: But sometimes it is a private thing; nobody is going to know about it. Then, especially, you can let it go. Say somebody comes to a class and is way below the level of the class. If he really wants to improve, he is not going to care about his grade: even if he fails, as long as he is improving and learning, he will be happy. A teacher who appreciates that maybe shouldn't send him to the higher class, but whatever: he can appreciate such a thing and definitely not punish him for not passing. That *rachmanus* is *davka* an intermediary between *chesed* and *gevura*, and it is *davka* a human thing, coming from a *daas*, a subjective thing.

And it is **the midda of Yaakov**. Yaakov says: I recognize that you have a potential and there is good, and I recognize that you have problems. What I want to do is come down and give you as much help as you need, but the objective is to get you to be able to go on your own.

blocks.title: A ladder out of the mud
blocks.text: It is like giving a person a ladder. You are not going to take him out of the mud and that's it; you are going to help him pull himself out. You will give him as much help as he needs to rehabilitate, until he can stand on his own. That is the thing of Yaakov, as is known.

sections.title: Yesod between netzach and hod: the kidneys that advise yes and no
sections.summary: *Netzach* and *hod* are the counsel on how to carry a decision out: *netzach* says to give and be proactive, *hod* to hold back and be cautious, like the kidneys that advise yes and no. *Yesod* decides between them, after the first decision of *daas*.

phrases.he: וכן בחינת יסוד
phrases.en: also *yesod*,

phrases.he: ממוצע לכלול ב' הפכים דנצח והוד

blocks.title: Spoon-feeding the student, or holding back
blocks.text:
So too *yesod* is the intermediary to include the two opposites of *netzach* and *hod*. Say you want to teach. *Netzach* is that since you want to bring out the idea to the student, you are going to do all the work for him. You will explain everything very simply and lay everything out, and that's it: he won't have to do any work. The good thing about that is that he will get it. The problem is that he is not really going to get to a higher level; he is not going to work and learn to think on his own. He will just become dependent on a good teacher.

*Hod* says that you want to inspire him to work and to go harder. So you are going to ask hard questions and make him think, and hold back some of the information, to keep it above him so that he feels there is something he wants to work to get.

phrases.he: שהוא ענין כליות יועצות
phrases.en: *netzach* and *hod* is like the kidneys that give advice,

phrases.he: הן ולאו
phrases.en: that they say yes and no.

phrases.he: קודם השפעת המשפיע
כשצריך להשפיע עצם המדות חסד וגבורה
phrases.en: then when you want to bring across *chesed* and *gevura*,

blocks.title: The kidney and the glands on top of it
blocks.text: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, that say yes and no. In the simple sense of "the kidneys advise", from what Rabbi Walters researched about it, there are three parts. In general, every organ the Torah talks about has three parts that correspond to *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*). So too the kidney: what is normally called the kidney in English is only the bottom third. On top of it are two adrenal glands, stacked one on top of the other. The top one is connected to the pituitary gland in the brain, and works together with the brain to regulate different things in the body.

sensitivity.reason: Describes the adrenal glands as two glands stacked on the kidney, the top one tied to the pituitary, as anatomy from his own research; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: *Netzach* and *hod* are *kelayos yo'atzos*, the kidneys that give advice, that say yes and no. In general, every organ the Torah talks about has three parts that correspond to *Chabad*, *chagas* and *nehi* (the three triads of *sefiros*), and so too the kidney.

blocks.title: Adrenaline and testosterone
blocks.text:
The middle one is not connected to the brain; it is connected to the emotional response. It gives off adrenaline, which gives a *hod* response. When a person is scared and thinks that something is bigger than him, he gets an adrenaline response: that is a thing of *hod*. That is what gives a person fight or flight, where he gives up hope, and so he is willing to give all of his *koach* away, because he has no other hope left. The *inyan* of *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice).

It also secretes testosterone, which is a thing of *netzach*: a person feels confident. That's why teenage boys, since they have a high testosterone level, are very cocky, not scared of dangerous things, always doing crazy stuff: it makes a person feel pumped up, that he can take on anything. That is a thing of *netzach*.

sensitivity.reason: Assigns adrenaline and testosterone to two stacked adrenal glands and ties them to hod and netzach as physiology; loose as medicine, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: When a person is scared and thinks that something is bigger than him, that is a thing of *hod*: he gives up hope, and so he is willing to give all of his *koach* away, because he has no other hope left. The *inyan* of *hod* is like *mesirus nefesh* (self-sacrifice). When a person feels confident and pumped up, that he can take on anything, like a teenager who is not scared of dangerous things and always doing crazy stuff, that is a thing of *netzach*.

blocks.text: And the actual kidney itself strains the blood, to say what is good and what is bad, which is on the level of *nehi*; just as the digestive system is like *netzach* and *hod*: yes and no. But the *inyan* is that *netzach* says yes and *hod* says no: *netzach* says to give, and *hod* to hold back.

Before the giver gives, **when you want to bring across chesed and gevura**: say you decide somebody is guilty. You have a verdict, but you don't have a sentence yet. You have to figure out what we are going to do with him. Or there is a problem: what are we going to do to fix it? You decided this is bad; how are we going to get rid of it? You have to figure out how to do that, and the *inyan* of *netzach* and *hod* is to figure out an *eitza* (counsel).

One gives counsel to be very proactive: that is *netzach*. *Hod* is to be more reserved, to be nervous and cautious. It is a healthy respect sometimes, depending on how strong it is. If somebody is cautious with, say, a gun, that is a *hod*: he has a *hoda'a* (acknowledgement) that it is a dangerous thing. But a person who has anxiety can be a negative: there is too much *hod*, and sometimes it is not good.

blocks.title: The zealots in the time of the Beis HaMikdash
blocks.text: And sometimes there is too much *netzach*. The *Biryonim* (the zealots) in the time of the *Beis HaMikdash* had too much *netzach*: they wanted to go fight, even though the correct thing to do would have been to wait it out. So there are these two sides: one says to be proactive and one says to be more passive; to go fight or to run away, whatever it is.

phrases.he: וכמו כל שיקול הדעת
phrases.en: and like every *shikul hadaas*

phrases.he: בא בהכרעה
ואחר הכרעה ישקול במאזני צדק שהן נצח והוד, איך להביא השפע למקבל כו'

blocks.text: Every *shikul hadaas* (weighing of the mind) comes to a decision. The whole middle line is an *inyan* of *shikul hadaas*: you have to weigh and make a judgment call. First there is a decision about the *etzem* thing, whether it is good or bad. Then you again have another decision, how to bring it out: that is the scales of justice, which are *netzach* and *hod*, how to bring the flow to the receiver.

sections.title: The middle line is one: it reaches the inner Keser, so it can join the two
sections.summary: *Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod* are one middle line, like the long bar through the boards of the *Mishkan*: on each level a personal decision between two poles. It can join the lines because it goes up to the inner *Keser*, the goal for which both sides are only tools.

phrases.he: והיינו כללות ענין קו האמצעי דת''י, שמחבר לב' קוין דימין ושמאל

blocks.text: This is the general *inyan* of the middle line of *daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod*. *Yesod* connects *netzach* and *hod*: how do you decide what to do? You decide with *yesod*, when you have a personal interest and connection. The real thing of a teacher is that he is sensitive to the student, he relates to him, and he tailor-makes the thing to the recipient. It is like the *inyan* of *hashgacha pratis* (individual Divine providence), a personalized connection. That is the *inyan* of *yesod*: it decides what is best between these two things in this situation.

So a *bar daas* (a person of understanding) is somebody who appreciates both sides, but is then also able to make a human, wise choice. You see people who can give good advice: that is the *inyan*. They see both sides, they understand where this person is holding and how these two methods will affect different situations, and what is best for this situation. That is the *inyan* of the middle line, which connects the two lines of right and left.

phrases.he: ופרטי התכללותן נקרא י''ב גבולי אלכסון כידוע,
phrases.en: And the particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines.

phrases.he: וקו האמצעי נקרא בריח התיכון
phrases.en: The middle line is called the support beam,

phrases.he: שמבריח מן הקצה כו'

blocks.title: The twelve edges of a cube
blocks.text: **The particular ways that they connect are called the twelve diagonal lines.** There are two different ways to count the twelve. One is that a cube has twelve edges. There are six sides, just like the six *middos*. If you are standing in the middle of the cube, you can go north, south, east and west, the four sides, and up and down: six. But you can also go diagonally, northeast or northwest, and there are twelve of them: four on the compass, another four up and another four down, like the twelve edges of a cube.

The other way, which is more what he is saying here: draw the *sefiros* like a *partzuf*, in the three lines. There are seven lines that connect the *sefiros* going up and down, three that connect them horizontally, and twelve that connect them diagonally. Those twelve are the ways they are included in each other. The last two are from *bina* to *netzach* and from *chachma* to *hod*.

blocks.title: The middle bar of the Mishkan
blocks.text:
**The middle line is called the support beam**, the *bariach hatichon* (the middle bar), which bolts from end to end. When you build a house, the support beam goes all the way through: you arrange the walls so that there are one or two points where it can go through. Or in the *Mishkan*: on the outside of the walls, on every side, at the top and the bottom, they had two bars that went through rings, and they had a hole drilled through the center of all the boards, with one long pole that went through all three walls. That was called the *bariach hatichon*; it went from end to end.

So if you look at the *Mishkan* sideways, the right and left lines are separate for each wall, but the middle line goes through everything and stays the same. The *bariach hatichon*, the middle line, is really one *inyan*.

*Daas*, *tiferes* and *yesod* are really like one *sefira*, and also *Keser* and *Malchus*: they are all really like one *sefira*, the middle line. It is all your personal decision. The only difference is that in *daas* you are making a decision in the intellect, in *tiferes* in the *middos*, and in *yesod* for *netzach* and *hod*. On each level you have two poles, and your personal decision is the middle line for each of them.

blocks.title: The dimmer switch
blocks.text: It is like a light switch that you can turn up and down. Essentially there is all the way off and all the way on, and where you decide to turn it is the middle line.

phrases.he: דהיינו שעולה עד בחינת פנימית הכתר,
phrases.en: and that's the *inyan* that it goes all the way to *pnimiyus haKeser*,

phrases.he: שלמעלה מהתחלקות הקוין
על כן יש בכחו לחבר ולכלול ב' הקוין כו'.
phrases.en: therefore it's able to connect.

blocks.text: That is, it goes all the way up to the *pnimiyus* of the *Keser*. That is why *davka* it can make the decision: the middle line is where you look deeper, into what you really want to accomplish. And when you look at what you really want to accomplish, you are able to find the best way to do it in this situation. Because you know where you are trying to go, you are able to go straight to it.

And that is higher than the division into lines. From that side you don't really care about *chesed* or *gevura*; it doesn't really matter. Those are all just tools, ways of accomplishing it, *keilim* (vessels): just a means to an end. Since you connect at the level of the end, you are able to find a compromise, whatever will accomplish your goal, because you are sensitive to that. This is why the *inyan* of *Tikun* really comes from higher than *Tohu*: it comes all the way from the *nekuda*, which is the *pnimiyus*.

So it has the power to join and include the two lines: since it's coming from *b'etzem* (in essence), it's higher than this *hischalkus* (division), **therefore it's able to connect**.

sections.title: The inner Keser: the revealed will and delight, with a hidden reason
sections.summary: *Keser sheb'Keser* is the will and delight that come out revealed, with ten *sefiros* of their own. Its *chachma* is the *ta'am kamus*, the hidden reason for the will, really a taste of delight; its *middos* are unlimited, an impossible dream, and are called the days of old next to the *middos* of *chachma* and *bina*.

phrases.he: וביאור ענין פנימית הכתר דנאצלים שנקרא כתר שבכתר (והוא בחינת כתר דעתיק יומין ואריך אנפין כו')
היינו בחינת הרצון והתענוג הבא בגלוי,
phrases.en: It's like when you have a revealed desire and a revealed pleasure.

phrases.he: שנקרא אור הכתר,
שגם הוא כלול מעשר ספירות
phrases.en: that this is also has ten *sefiros*.

blocks.text: The explanation of the *pnimiyus* of the *Keser* of *Atzilus*, called *Keser sheb'Keser*: this is like the *Akudim* (the bound lights), the single *nekuda* from before, which includes everything. It is the will and the delight that come out revealed: like when you have a revealed desire and a revealed pleasure. And this too has ten *sefiros*.

phrases.he: ובחינת חכמה שבכתר זהו הטעם לרצון
phrases.en: the *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the *ratzon*.

phrases.he: ונקרא טעם כמוס לרצון

blocks.text: The *chachma* of the *Keser* is the reason for the will, and it is called a *ta'am kamus* (a hidden reason) for the will. Here he is talking about the reason that comes after the will. Rabbi Walters thinks the reason it is called hidden is that the will usually covers over the reason. Even when you make a reason for it, it is not really for the reason; it is not the real reason. The will covers it over.

The other reason it is called hidden is that the *pnimiyus* of the *ta'am* comes from *ta'am* in the sense of delight: a taste, the *geshmak* (relish) that you get. The reason you want this *davka* is that it gives you a certain *geshmak*, a certain special *taanug* (delight) that you get in this, and that is what you are looking for.

blocks.title: Why that flavor ice cream?
blocks.text: So the form you find for your will is the reason you like it. Ask a person, "Why did you pick that flavor ice cream?" "Well, 'cause it's more chocolatey." So what? That doesn't explain why you should want it; that's just telling me what it is. You are looking for a certain taste, a certain *geshmak*, and the reason that comes out is really just trying to pinpoint what aspect is the thing that you want.

phrases.he: וכן יש בו חסד ונצח
phrases.en: and it also has *chesed* and *netzach*,

phrases.he: והכל בבחינת הרצון שהוא בלתי מוגבל,
phrases.en: and the *ratzon*, it's not limited.

phrases.he: גם שבא בגלוי מעצם העלם הרצון כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: And it also has *chesed* and *netzach*: everything is in the will. And it is all in the way of the will, which is not limited, even though it came out revealed from the essential concealment of the will. It already went through *Adam Kadmon*, and it became a will for a particular thing: instead of being a will for a home, it is now a will for a house. But it is still unlimited; it is still unreasonable.

blocks.title: The impossible mansion
blocks.text: You want a house: something realistic, tangible, a physical thing. In theory it is desirable in the physical world. But the way it is in the *Keser*, he wants a mansion that is totally impossible to get, a huge palace that is infinitely big and infinitely rich, and it's impossible. The same with everything: from the side of the essential will, a person's *chesed*, say his love for his kid, is really an infinite thing. He wants to be a *mashpia* (giver) infinitely good.

phrases.he: ועל כן המדות שברצון ותענוג נקרא ימי קדם
phrases.en: that's why they're called the olden days.

phrases.he: לגבי מדות שבחכמה ובינה
phrases.en: compared to the *middos* that come in *chachma* and *bina*

phrases.he: שבאים בהגבלה כפי הגבלת השכל הגלוי בלבד
כמו שיתבאר,
phrases.en: like we'll explain,

phrases.he: עד בחינת מלכות שבכתר
phrases.en: until *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

blocks.text: So the *middos* in the will and delight are called *yemei kedem*: that's why they're called the olden days. Like everything was bigger in the olden days: in the olden days you went ten miles to school, and both ways were uphill. "I don't know, maybe it's connected; it's interesting that they call them old."

Compared to the *middos* that come in *chachma* and *bina*, where you think what is practical, these are called *kedem*: your primal thing, your essential desire before you start being practical. The *ratzon kadum* (the primordial will) is called the days of old compared to *Adam Kadmon*, and this is also called the days of old compared to *chachma* and *bina*, because it is your dream, your original dream. Then *chachma* and *bina* bring it down to scale, to what is possible to get: they come in limitation, by the limits of the revealed intellect alone, as will be explained, down to *Malchus sheb'Keser*.

sections.title: Above the division: the will with no reason, and the curtain before it
sections.summary: The outer *Keser* divides into lines because a reason gives the will a form, with better and worse. The *Keser sheb'Keser* is a simple will with no reason, all or nothing, like G-d's "Be silent, so it arose in thought". The *paroches* between it and *chachma* is where the will takes a form, so prayer goes before it to change judgement to kindness.

phrases.he: ומבחינת חיצוניות דכתר נחלק לג' קוין
phrases.en: and from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* though it already divides into three *kavin*.

phrases.he: מפני שבטעם הכמוס לרצון נקרא התחלקות הרצון לחסד וגבורה וממוצע כו'

blocks.text: But from the *chitzoniyus* of the *Keser* it already divides into three lines, because in the hidden reason for the will the division of the will into *chesed*, *gevura* and an intermediary is recognizable. (He reads the text's *nikra*, "is called", as *nikar*, "is recognizable".)

Once you already make a *tzura* (form) of what you want, which is the *inyan* of the reason, there is already a certain thing you like and a certain thing you don't like; something can be better or worse, closer or farther away. And the *inyan* of your *chachma* and *bina* is to figure out what you can practically get that will be the best, the closest match to your will. So from the *chitzoniyus* it already has a form. Even though it is an unpractical form, you can already say, "Okay, I want a huge mansion, so we'll get you the biggest thing we can find." From that side you can already have a *Tikun* thing, a decision on the three lines.

phrases.he: אבל בכתר שבכתר שלמעלה מטעם כמוס לרצון עדיין,
phrases.en: but the *Keser* *Keser* is higher than any particular *ratzon*,

phrases.he: רק רצון פשוט ועצמי בלא טעם כלל
כי אין טעם לרצון כלל, גם לא טעם כמוס

blocks.text: But the *Keser sheb'Keser* is higher than any particular will: only a simple, essential will, with no reason at all. From the side of the essential will, there is no *inyan* of a compromise. It is all or nothing: as far as your actual goal, your inner goal, either you got it or you didn't. So it has no reason at all.

For there is no reason for the will at all. Why do you want it? The real inner thing that you wanted, you just want it because you want it. Once you start figuring out that you want it like this, you attach your essential will to a particular form.

blocks.title: The will for money and the get-rich-quick tapes
blocks.text: This is not really an essential will, but relatively: say the will for money. That is the essential will, in a *nekuda*, higher than every reason: you want it because you want it. Then in the *chitzoniyus* of the will, the *chachma* and *bina* start to make a picture of how you are going to get it, say a business deal. You start imagining that you are going to do this deal, and you go to one of these get-rich-quick tapes and they get you all psyched up on how much money you are going to make. You are already making a particular way you want to get it. Even if it is a totally impractical dream that the person is dreaming up, it is already coming into a line.

He is already considering that there is something he wants, and certain things are going to be closer and things will be far away, so he has to make it in a certain form *davka*, so that it will fit the will. But from the side of the essential will it is not like that: only a simple, essential will, with no reason at all, for there is no reason in the will at all, not even a hidden reason.

phrases.he: כענין שתוק כך עלה במחשבה כו', וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר

blocks.text: Like "Be silent, so it arose in thought", said of the ten martyrs of the kingdom: that is not a thing to compromise on; that is what He wanted. If it were a means to an end, you could say, "Well, I have a better way for you to do it," and there could be a compromise. But since it was the actual thing He wanted, there is none.

Like the whole *inyan* of "This is the statute of the Torah" by the *para aduma* (the red heifer). One of the explanations the Rebbe gives is that the whole *inyan* of why you need a *yerida* (a descent) for an *aliya* (an ascent) is the *inyan* of the *chok* (a commandment done just because G-d said so). Why the one person has to become *tamei* (impure) to make the other *tahor* (pure): we understand it makes sense, the way the world works, that to have an ascent you have to have a descent.

blocks.title: Profit and the sink
blocks.text: If you want to make a profit, you have to invest money. If you are going to fix your sink, you are going to get your hands dirty. Fine, that's the way it works.

blocks.question: Why did G-d have to make it that way?
blocks.text: G-d did not have to make it so that we gain only through pain, "no pain, no gain". He could have made it that we have all the virtues. All these things say *nahama d'kisufa* (the bread of shame), but G-d could have given us the virtue without that. He didn't have to do it that way. So that is the *chok*: G-d chose that He wanted to do it like this. That is the real essential will, the essential delight, that it should be such a thing. That is here the fiftieth gate: the essential thing, which is not something you can describe, as explained elsewhere.

phrases.he: על כן הוא למעלה מהתחלקות ימין ושמאל כו', הגם שבא בגלוי מבחינת האחרונה שבהעלם הרצון דבחינת אדם קדמון (כנזכר לעיל בסוף אות י''ט)

blocks.question: "Wait a minute, but it already has an order from *Adam Kadmon*. *Adam Kadmon* already makes three lines."
blocks.text: So it is above the division into right and left, even though it comes out revealed from the last level of the concealed will of *Adam Kadmon*. Take the example of the will for money. By the time you came to a will for money, you had already made three lines in *Adam Kadmon*, to figure out your self-image: from your essential desire to be happy you created an image of prosperity, of which being rich is a part. So it has already divided up into lines.

It is true that relative to the essential will before *Adam Kadmon* it became lines. But once it comes out, relative to what comes after, those become like an essential will again. That is the *inyan* of *gilui ha'helem* (revelation of what is hidden): the essence becomes connected with this thing. And as long as that does not change, it has the full force of an essential will; that is actually what you want. You want happiness; if your *Adam Kadmon* tells you that happiness means money, then you want money, *nekuda*, as they say in Hebrew. And that is not negotiable.

The same thing is how a Jew can have *mesirus nefesh* for a *mitzva* (a commandment). What a Jew really wants is to be connected to G-d. If a prophet would tell you to transgress any *mitzva* in the Torah, you would do it; it would actually be a *mitzva* to do it. So you do not essentially want to keep Shabbos: if a prophet would tell you to desecrate Shabbos, it would be a *mitzva* to desecrate Shabbos. Or say it is a matter of *pikuach nefesh* (danger to life): it is a *mitzva* to desecrate Shabbos.

So how can a Jew, if a *goy* says, "I'm gonna shoot you if you're not *mechalel Shabbos*," have *mesirus nefesh* for it? Because as long as, in this situation, the Torah says that this is connected to G-d, it has the full force of his will to be connected to G-d. Where the Torah tells a Jew that this is not connected to his connection to G-d, he can do it and still be connected. But if a Jew associates the two, then the full force of his *yechida* (the essence of the soul) is connected to every deed he does, and it becomes totally non-negotiable: just the essential will, and not the three *mochin* at all.

phrases.he: ועל זה אמר והבדילה הפרוכת בין הקדש כו'
phrases.en: the *paroches* separates between the *Kodesh* and the *Kodesh Kodashim*,

phrases.he: בחינת פרסא שבין כתר דכתר לחכמה כו'
והוא בחינת קרומא דאוירא
phrases.en: This is the membrane of air, the arachnoid membrane in the brain, it's called,

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר באריכות

blocks.text: About this it says, "The *paroches* (the curtain) shall separate between the Holy" and the Holy of Holies: between the *Keser* of *Keser*, which is the essential will, and the way you bring it out, the *chachma* of the will, where it already has a form. There is a *masach* (a screen). It is the *parsa* (the partition) between *Keser* of *Keser* and *chachma*.

It is the *kruma d'avira*, the membrane of air, called the arachnoid membrane in the brain, as is written elsewhere at length. We are going to talk about it in chapter 25, where you can talk about the hairs, and *Atik*, and the thirteen tikkunim of the beard of *Arich*, things like that.

blocks.title: The fluid of delight under the skull
blocks.text: The point is that in a person physically there is a liquid under the skull, called in medicine, he thinks, the subdural fluid, and that liquid is the essential delight: it gives a person the essential feeling of delight and will. But usually it does not come down in pure form. There is a spongy membrane that holds it, with little hair-like tubes that inject it into the brain. When a certain part of the brain is active, it draws more liquid into that part, and it stimulates that part of the brain; and when it drips on the back of the spine it gives the person delight.

sensitivity.reason: Says a fluid under the skull is the source of delight, injected into the brain and dripping on the spine, as medical fact; not what medicine says, and a reader may take it as fact.
sensitivity.publishable: The point is that the essential delight does not come down to the faculties in its pure form. There is a membrane that holds it and lets it through, and wherever a faculty is active, more of the delight is drawn into it and stimulates it.

blocks.title: Each person's membrane, each person's nature
blocks.text: It drips according to the shape of this membrane, and each person has a slightly different shaped membrane. That is what gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at certain things, because it is easier for him to get delight from certain parts of his brain, from certain forms, than from others. That is the *inyan* of the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*: *mazal* comes from *nozel*, flowing, which we can talk about in chapter 25.

sensitivity.reason: Continues the physiology of the brain fluid, making the shape of the membrane the cause of a person's nature, as medical fact.
sensitivity.publishable: The delight comes through according to the shape of this membrane, and each person's is a little different. That is what gives a person his nature: he enjoys certain things more and is better at certain things, because it is easier for him to get delight from certain forms than from others. That is the *inyan* of the *mazal* (lit. a flow), the *mazalos*: *mazal* comes from *nozel*, flowing, which we can talk about in chapter 25.

blocks.text: So the point is that this *masach* is what connects: you have to create a thing that connects your essential will to a form. To go from the essential will to the means to the end, you have to have this thing, as is written elsewhere at length.

phrases.he: ועל כן אומר יהי רצון מלפניך, מלפני הפרסא כו'
לשנות מרצון של דין לרצון של חסד וכהאי גוונא כו' ודי למבין:

blocks.text: So one says, "May it be the will before You", before the *parsa*. When we want to change something, we *davka* want to connect to the essential will, higher than any form. Inside that, it can come out in any form: G-d can accomplish the same thing in a totally different way, and it doesn't have to be *davka* this way. But once it comes through the *paroches*, it gets set. It has to be in a certain form, because that is already a reason for the will.

To change from a will of *din* to a will of *chesed*, and the like, and this is enough for one who understands. That is why *davka* the essential will, the essence of the *Keser*, can change from *din* to *chesed*: it can really do it either way. That is the *inyan* of the three *mochin*.

reviewQuestions.question: Why does *chachma* lean towards *chesed* and *bina* towards *gevura*? Use the gift and the person who is "just misguided".
Why is *netzach* "separate" from *chesed*, and what does *mivtzaim* in the cold show about it?
What does *daas* do with the two ways of looking at a person, and why can a computer not do it?
How is *tiferes* like mercy after the verdict, and what is the attribute of Yaakov?
Why can the middle line join the two lines, and what does the middle bar of the *Mishkan* show about it?
Why is there no compromise in the *Keser sheb'Keser*, and why does prayer go "before the *parsa*"?

notes.text: Line 27: he reads "it is Keser of Adam Kadmon" (79 w1465-1477) where the text has "Keser of Atik Yomin and Arich Anpin"; and in line 28 he reads "which is called Arich Anpin" (79 w1494-1502) where the text has "called the light of the Keser". The block follows the chapter's text and his explanation (the Akudim, the single nekuda) without naming either reading.
Line 34: he reads the text's nikra as nikar ("recognizable") and says it is "supposed to be" so (79 w2223-2241); the block says so. The transcript hears the two words the same and is garbled here.

The physiology in classes 78 (the kidney and adrenal glands, adrenaline and testosterone, 78 w2122-2423) and 80 (a fluid under the skull, which he calls subdural, as the essential delight dripping on the spine, 80 w1368-1606) is kept as he gave it, with his own hedges ("from what I researched", "I think"). It is loose as anatomy (the adrenal glands are not two glands stacked on the kidney; the subdural space normally holds no fluid; the fluid around the brain is cerebrospinal fluid, under the arachnoid). Those blocks are flagged health-or-legal, as chapter 15 flags his medical claims, with publishable texts that keep the hod/netzach and the membrane points.

Phrases he reads without translating keep their Hebrew alone: the start of line 1, line 2 up to Keser sheb'Keser (he explains it instead), the end of line 3 and all of line 4, the end of line 7 (b'davar murkav, which he glosses as "not an etzem chesed"), the end of line 8, the end of line 9, the start of lines 11 and 13, lines 14, 16 and 23 (read whole, then explained), most of line 15 and line 19, the middle of line 20, the end of line 21, line 22, the end of line 24, the end of line 25, line 27 and the middle of line 28, the end of line 29 and of line 31, the middle of line 32, line 34, the end of line 35, all of line 36 (his "why do you want it? You want it because you want it" explains it rather than translating it), lines 37 and 38, line 40, the end of line 41, and lines 42-43. The English of line 13 ("it's davka the middle thing, which is daas", 78 w366-373) is from his summary after the opening question; the end of line 12 (78 w6-14) is from class 78's opening, and the English of the end of line 20 is from class 79's opening (79 w11-20). The English of line 26 is the end of the sentence right after his reading of it (79 w1460-1464); the first half of that sentence ("since it's coming from b'etzem, it's higher than this hischalkus") gives the reason and belongs to line 25, so it is in the block, not the phrase.

In the mesirus nefesh block (80 w1142-1176) the transcript has "the whole inyan of shin-samech-heh kedushos", which is garbled (perhaps the 365 prohibitions); the block keeps only his point that the Torah tells a Jew where a deed is not connected to his connection to G-d.

"Be silent, so it arose in thought" (line 37): he ties it to the ten martyrs of the kingdom (80 w388-416); the Gemara (Menachos 29b) says it of Rabbi Akiva's death, one of the ten. The block keeps his words. "That is here the fiftieth gate" (80 w717-737) is kept as he said it; the transcript has "sha'ar nun".

The goy in the halachic case of being forced to desecrate Shabbos (80 w1079-1106) is flagged other-groups, as the series flags the word wherever it occurs (chapters 15, 17, 18, 28); the publishable text says "a non-Jew", which keeps the halachic case. The remark itself is neutral, so an editor may decide the word can stand.
